analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to document and prove their mental health coverage limits are no stricter than medical ones.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a bipartisan lead pair and five cosponsors, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires insurers to cover mental health and substance use care on equal terms with physical care. But insurers can quietly make mental care harder to get using rules that aren't simple dollar caps — things like prior authorization, narrow provider networks, and limits on how many therapy visits you get. This bill would force health plans to put together a detailed written analysis showing those hidden limits are no more restrictive for mental health than for medical care, hand it over to federal regulators on request, and submit to random annual audits of at least 50 plans, with repeat violations reported to inspectors general and the states.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who need mental health or substance use treatment — therapy, psychiatric care, addiction treatment — and currently face obstacles like prior authorization, narrow networks, and visit limits that physical care doesn't face. Their families and employers, who pay for coverage that often doesn't deliver mental care when it's needed, also benefit from the added transparency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People seeking mental health and addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans covering both medical and mental health benefits to perform and produce comparative analyses of nonquantitative treatment limitations — non-number limits like prior authorization and network rules — showing they are applied no more stringently to mental health and substance use benefits than to medical and surgical benefits.

Sets a compliance process: plans must make the analyses available to the Secretary of Health and Human Services within 60 days starting in 2020 and immediately starting in 2021; the Secretary must request analyses from any plan with complaints against it and from at least 50 randomly selected plans every year.

Requires the Secretary to tell noncompliant plans exactly what to fix, share findings with the HHS, Labor, and Treasury inspectors general and with states, publish deidentified noncompliance examples, and report annually to the relevant congressional committees with the analyses attached.

Applies the same requirements across employer plans under ERISA and the tax code, and to individual and group insurance under the Public Health Service Act, closing the main routes plans use to avoid parity enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and the employers and insurers that sponsor them, which would bear the cost of preparing detailed comparative analyses, responding to regulator requests and random audits, and changing plan rules when the analysis shows mental health benefits are treated more stringently. Some of that cost could be passed to premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill is paperwork-and-enforcement only: it does not set new coverage standards or add funding for mental health care, so if insurers' hidden limits are formally comparable on paper but care remains hard to get in practice, the analyses would not fix it.

Compliance costs fall on plans and their employer sponsors, and the requirement to produce detailed analyses on 60 days' notice — then immediately, from 2021 — imposes real administrative burdens, particularly on smaller employers and self-insured plans.

The bill directs regulators to identify noncompliance and specify required corrective actions but does not itself create new penalties or a private right of action, so enforcement still depends on regulators choosing to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — forcing plans to prove, in writing and under audit, that mental health care isn't quietly harder to get than physical care — addresses a documented gap in how parity rules work, since limits like prior authorization and network size are exactly the ones regulators historically couldn't see. The main costs are administrative compliance for plans and the risk that paper comparability doesn't translate into real access. On balance a modest, targeted transparency measure whose cost is small relative to what it asks insurers to disclose.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 5, 2019 by Senator Chris Murphy, joined by Senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
It had five cosponsors: three Democrats and two Republicans.
No further action was taken: the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no committee report, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off: they never had to produce comparative analyses proving their mental health limits match their medical limits, so the hidden restrictions on mental health and addiction care stayed in place, and the status quo of weak parity enforcement continued.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require plans to document parity of nonquantitative mental health treatment limits.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Senator Murphy on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never held a markup, reported it, or allowed it to advance during the remaining 19 months of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, so it never advanced to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The lead pair was bipartisan — Democrat Murphy and Republican Cassidy — and the five cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans; nothing in the record shows opposition along party lines, and the bill died in committee without any vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans would have to prepare detailed comparative analyses proving hidden limits on mental health care — prior authorization, network rules, visit limits — are no stricter than for medical care, and face random annual audits and corrective-action demands when they fail. Insurers benefit today from these less-visible limits, which are the main tool for keeping mental health and addiction care costs down, so their interest in the bill runs against patients who need that care.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: If hidden plan limits were forced into the open and corrected, therapists, psychiatrists, and addiction treatment programs would see fewer denials, narrower networks, and visit caps, and more patients able to pay for care.
